prog-dai-001.question: A 58-year-old man is resuscitated from ventricular fibrillation occurring outside the setting of an acute myocardial infarction. Work-up reveals no reversible cause. What is the recommended management?
options: Long-term amiodarone, with rhythm reassessment at 3 months
Implantation of a secondary prevention ICD
Long-term wearable defibrillator (LifeVest) instead of an ICD
Implantable loop recorder to document any recurrence
commentaires: Incorrect: antiarrhythmic drugs alone, including amiodarone, are inferior to the ICD in terms of mortality after VF without a reversible cause.
Correct: VF without a reversible cause and life expectancy > 1 year = secondary prevention ICD, class I (ESC 2022).
Incorrect: the vest is only a temporary bridge when implantation has to be deferred, never a long-term solution.
Incorrect: the arrhythmia is already documented and it is lethal; there is nothing further to document, the patient needs protection.
prog-dai-001.explication: This is the original and most robust indication for an ICD: secondary prevention after VF or haemodynamically poorly tolerated VT without a reversible cause (class I, level A in the 2022 ESC guidelines), provided that life expectancy with good functional status exceeds one year. Antiarrhythmic drugs alone, including amiodarone, are inferior to the ICD in terms of mortality in this setting. The wearable defibrillator is only a temporary solution for a patient who cannot be implanted straight away. An implantable loop recorder has no role here: the arrhythmia is already documented and it is lethal.
prog-dai-001.aRetenir: VF or poorly tolerated VT without a reversible cause = secondary prevention ICD (class I).

prog-dai-002.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, which of these patients with coronary artery disease has a class I indication for a primary prevention ICD?
options: Myocardial infarction 10 days ago, LVEF 30%, asymptomatic on treatment
Coronary artery disease, NYHA I, LVEF 40%, no non-sustained VT on Holter
Coronary artery disease, NYHA II, LVEF 32% after more than 3 months of optimal therapy
Coronary artery disease, refractory NYHA IV, not a candidate for transplant or LVAD
commentaires: Incorrect: within 40 days of a myocardial infarction, LVEF may recover and early implantation has not reduced mortality; reassess later.
Incorrect: with an LVEF of 40% and nothing else, there is no indication for a primary prevention ICD.
Correct: coronary artery disease, NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy = class I (MADIT-II, SCD-HeFT).
Incorrect: in refractory NYHA IV with no plan for transplantation, LVAD or CRT, the ICD does not alter prognosis.
prog-dai-002.explication: The class I primary prevention indication applies to symptomatic patients with coronary artery disease (NYHA II–III) and an LVEF ≤ 35% despite at least 3 months of optimal medical therapy, based on MADIT-II and SCD-HeFT. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines confirm this indication (class I, level B1), provided expected survival is > 1 year with good functional status. Shortly after myocardial infarction, LVEF may still improve and trials of early implantation showed no mortality benefit: an ICD is not recommended within 40 days (class III), and LVEF is reassessed later on optimal therapy. With an LVEF of 40% and nothing else, there is no indication. A patient in refractory NYHA class IV, with no plan for CRT, LVAD or transplantation, has no indication (class III): the ICD does not alter a prognosis dominated by end-stage heart failure.
prog-dai-002.aRetenir: Coronary artery disease, NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy = primary prevention ICD (class I, ESC 2022 and ESC 2026 HF).

prog-dai-003.question: True or false: in the 2022 ESC guidelines, a primary prevention ICD in non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of optimal therapy) is a class I recommendation, just as it is in ischaemic heart disease.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is false. It is class I in coronary artery disease, but in non-ischaemic DCM the 2022 ESC guidelines (like the 2026 ESC HF guidelines) give only class IIa.
Correct: non-ischaemic DCM, LVEF ≤ 35% = class IIa, notably since DANISH (no reduction in all-cause mortality).
prog-dai-003.explication: False: in non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy, this indication is class IIa ("should be considered"). The downgrade is explained in particular by the DANISH trial: the ICD reduced sudden death but not all-cause mortality in these patients, most of whom also received CRT, with a benefit that appeared to be confined to younger patients. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines maintain this distinction: class I (level B1) for ischaemic aetiology and IIa (level B1) for non-ischaemic aetiology, while noting that a meta-analysis nonetheless found an overall survival benefit. The decision must therefore take into account age, comorbidities, the risk of non-sudden death and other risk markers (late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, genetics), through shared decision-making.
prog-dai-003.aRetenir: Non-ischaemic DCM, LVEF ≤ 35%: ICD is class IIa (not I) since DANISH, confirmed by the 2026 ESC HF guidelines.

prog-dai-004.question: In a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy and LVEF < 50%, which of the following are among the risk markers that, according to the 2022 ESC guidelines, may lead to consideration of a primary prevention ICD (at least two are required)?
options: Unexplained syncope
Late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI
An isolated truncating variant in the TTN (titin) gene
Sustained monomorphic VT inducible at programmed ventricular stimulation
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
commentaires: Correct: unexplained syncope is one of the risk factors recognised by the 2022 ESC guidelines in DCM.
Correct: late gadolinium enhancement (fibrosis) on MRI is a recognised arrhythmic risk marker.
Incorrect: the high-risk genes listed are LMNA, PLN, FLNC and RBM20; TTN variants, which are common, carry a lower arrhythmic risk.
Correct: inducible sustained monomorphic VT at programmed ventricular stimulation is one of the criteria.
Incorrect: paroxysmal AF is not a criterion; it mainly predisposes to inappropriate shocks.
prog-dai-004.explication: The 2022 ESC guidelines broadened risk stratification in DCM beyond LVEF alone: with an LVEF < 50%, the presence of at least two risk factors (unexplained syncope, late gadolinium enhancement on MRI, inducible sustained monomorphic VT, a pathogenic variant in a high-risk gene: LMNA, PLN, FLNC or RBM20) leads to consideration of an ICD (class IIa). For LMNA variant carriers, there is also a dedicated risk score. Truncating titin (TTN) variants, the most common in DCM, are not on this list of high-risk genes. Paroxysmal AF is not a criterion: it is mainly a source of inappropriate shocks. The classic pitfall is to reason solely on the basis of the 35% threshold.
prog-dai-004.aRetenir: In DCM, high-risk genetics (LMNA, PLN, FLNC, RBM20), MRI and syncope count as much as LVEF.

prog-dai-005.question: True or false: ICD implantation is recommended only if life expectancy with good functional status exceeds one year.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: this condition applies across all ICD indications in the European guidelines.
Incorrect: without a life expectancy > 1 year with good functional status, the ICD exposes the patient to complications and shocks with no survival benefit.
prog-dai-005.explication: True: this condition applies across all ICD indications in the European guidelines. The ICD prevents arrhythmic death but does nothing to change the course of metastatic cancer, end-stage heart failure with no treatment plan or advanced dementia. In these patients, it exposes them to complications and shocks with no survival benefit. The assessment must be holistic and shared with the patient.
prog-dai-005.aRetenir: No ICD if life expectancy with good functional status is less than one year.

prog-dai-006.question: True or false: in SCD-HeFT (heart failure patients in NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 35%, ischaemic and non-ischaemic), amiodarone reduced mortality to a similar extent as the ICD.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: in SCD-HeFT, amiodarone provided no survival benefit compared with placebo.
Correct: only the ICD reduced all-cause mortality (by about 23% compared with placebo); amiodarone did not.
prog-dai-006.explication: False. SCD-HeFT randomised 2,521 patients to placebo, amiodarone or a conservatively programmed single-chamber ICD (shock only, single zone from 188 bpm). The ICD reduced all-cause mortality by about 23% compared with placebo, whereas amiodarone provided no benefit. Together with MADIT-II, it is one of the two pillars of the primary prevention indication. A classic pitfall is to believe that amiodarone can replace the ICD: it does not improve survival in this population.
prog-dai-006.aRetenir: SCD-HeFT: the ICD reduces mortality, amiodarone does not.

prog-dai-007.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, in which situation should a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (LifeVest-type vest) be considered (class IIa)?
options: Secondary prevention ICD indicated, implantation deferred
Elderly ICD recipient who no longer wishes to receive shocks
Recurrent vasovagal syncope in a young person with a normal heart
Any patient within 40 days of myocardial infarction with LVEF ≤ 35%
commentaires: Correct: this is the typical bridging use (class IIa), for example after extraction for endocarditis while awaiting reimplantation.
Incorrect: a vest makes no sense in a patient who refuses shocks; deactivation of therapies should be discussed instead.
Incorrect: reflex syncope does not carry a risk of arrhythmic death and does not warrant any defibrillator.
Incorrect: in the early post-infarction period, the vest is considered only on a case-by-case basis (IIb); VEST did not reduce arrhythmic death.
prog-dai-007.explication: The wearable defibrillator is a bridging solution. The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend considering it (IIa) in adults who have a secondary prevention ICD indication but cannot be implanted straight away, typically after extraction for infection. In the early post-infarction period, it may be considered only on a case-by-case basis (IIb): the VEST trial did not show a significant reduction in arrhythmic death, its primary endpoint. It has no role in reflex syncope or in a patient who refuses shocks.
prog-dai-007.aRetenir: LifeVest = temporary bridge, mainly for secondary prevention when implantation is deferred.

prog-dai-008.question: True or false: a conscious patient wearing a wearable defibrillator (LifeVest) can prevent a shock from being delivered by pressing the response buttons when the alarm sounds.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: a conscious patient can press the response buttons to withhold the shock; once unconscious, they can no longer do so and the shock is delivered.
Incorrect: the response buttons exist precisely to avoid shocking a conscious patient (artefact, well-tolerated arrhythmia).
prog-dai-008.explication: True: when an arrhythmia is detected, the vest issues alarms (vibration, sound, voice message). A conscious patient can then press the response buttons to delay or withhold the shock. This principle avoids shocking a conscious patient, for example in the event of artefact or a well-tolerated arrhythmia. A patient who has lost consciousness can no longer press the buttons, and the shock is delivered. Educating the patient and those around them (not to press the buttons on the patient's behalf) is essential.
prog-dai-008.aRetenir: LifeVest: a conscious patient can withhold the shock; an unconscious patient is shocked.

prog-dai-009.question: What are the limitations of the subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) that make it unsuitable for some patients?
options: It does not deliver ATP
It does not provide permanent bradycardia pacing
It cannot deliver shocks above 20 J
It is contraindicated after previous endocarditis
commentaires: Correct: the S-ICD does not offer ATP, which makes it unsuitable for recurrent monomorphic VT that is reliably terminated by ATP.
Correct: apart from brief post-shock pacing, it provides no bradycardia pacing.
Incorrect: it delivers high-energy shocks, up to 80 J.
Incorrect: a history of transvenous device infection is, on the contrary, an argument in its favour.
prog-dai-009.explication: The S-ICD has no transvenous lead: the lead is tunnelled subcutaneously alongside the sternum. It delivers high-energy shocks (80 J), well above 20 J, but offers neither ATP nor permanent bradycardia pacing, apart from brief post-shock pacing. It is therefore unsuitable for patients who need pacing, CRT or ATP (recurrent monomorphic VT reliably terminated by ATP). Conversely, a history of transvenous device infection or difficult venous access are good arguments in its favour.
prog-dai-009.aRetenir: S-ICD: no ATP and no permanent pacing, so reserved for patients with no pacing needs.

prog-dai-010.question: Regarding the ECG screening test performed before subcutaneous ICD implantation, which statements are correct?
options: It checks that at least one sensing vector offers an acceptable QRS/T-wave ratio
It must be performed both supine and standing
It is used to estimate the defibrillation threshold before implantation
A failed screen is simply corrected by lowering sensitivity after implantation
commentaires: Correct: that is the purpose of screening, to check that at least one vector gives a QRS that is large relative to the T wave.
Correct: signal morphology varies with posture, hence testing supine and standing.
Incorrect: screening says nothing about defibrillation efficacy, which is checked in the implant room.
Incorrect: a failed screen predisposes to double counting (QRS + T wave) and inappropriate shocks; it is not something to be fixed by programming afterwards.
prog-dai-010.explication: The S-ICD senses cardiac activity on subcutaneous vectors that resemble a surface ECG. Screening, manual or automated, checks that at least one vector gives a QRS complex of good amplitude relative to the T wave, in several positions (supine, standing), since morphology changes with posture. A patient who fails screening is exposed to double counting (QRS + T wave) and inappropriate shocks: this is a reason not to implant, not a problem to be solved later by programming. Screening has nothing to do with defibrillation efficacy, which is checked in the implant room.
prog-dai-010.aRetenir: S-ICD screening checks sensing (QRS/T ratio in several positions), not defibrillation.

prog-dai-011.question: What was the main finding of the PRAETORIAN trial comparing the subcutaneous ICD with the transvenous ICD (patients with no pacing indication)?
options: Non-inferiority for the composite of complications + inappropriate shocks
Early termination of the trial for excess complications in the S-ICD arm
Significant reduction in all-cause mortality in the S-ICD arm
More ineffective appropriate shocks with the S-ICD than with the transvenous ICD
commentaires: Correct: the S-ICD was non-inferior, with fewer lead-related complications and a trend towards more inappropriate shocks.
Incorrect: the trial ran to completion; the S-ICD actually had fewer lead-related complications.
Incorrect: PRAETORIAN was neither designed nor powered for mortality.
Incorrect: shock efficacy was not found wanting; the difference concerned complications and inappropriate shocks.
prog-dai-011.explication: PRAETORIAN randomised 849 patients with an ICD indication and no pacing indication. The S-ICD was non-inferior to the transvenous ICD for the composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks. The two components moved in opposite directions: fewer lead complications with the S-ICD, and a trend towards more inappropriate shocks, often due to oversensing. The trial was not designed for mortality. These data support the ESC 2022 class IIa recommendation for the S-ICD when neither pacing, CRT nor ATP is needed.
prog-dai-011.aRetenir: PRAETORIAN: S-ICD non-inferior to transvenous ICD (fewer lead complications, but not fewer inappropriate shocks).

prog-dai-012.question: What is the primary role of an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)?
options: To treat atrial fibrillation by automatic cardioversion
To detect and automatically treat VT and VF
To continuously measure pulmonary artery pressure
To replace beta-blocker therapy in heart failure
commentaires: Incorrect: the ICD does not routinely treat AF; indeed, AF is a common cause of inappropriate shocks.
Correct: the ICD monitors ventricular rhythm and treats VT and VF with ATP or a shock.
Incorrect: that is the role of dedicated sensors (such as CardioMEMS), not an ICD.
Incorrect: medical therapy remains essential, notably to limit the number of episodes.
prog-dai-012.explication: The ICD continuously monitors ventricular rhythm. When it recognises VT or VF, it automatically treats it with ATP (antitachycardia pacing) or an electrical shock. It also provides bradycardia pacing like a pacemaker. It does not routinely treat AF and does not replace medical therapy, which remains essential to limit the number of episodes.
prog-dai-012.aRetenir: The ICD automatically detects and treats VT and VF (ATP or shock).

prog-dai-013.question: An ICD records a tachycardia with a regular ventricular cycle length of 300 ms. What rate does this correspond to?
options: 150 bpm
180 bpm
200 bpm
240 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: 150 bpm corresponds to a cycle length of 400 ms (60,000 / 400).
Incorrect: 180 bpm corresponds to a cycle length of about 333 ms.
Incorrect: 240 bpm corresponds to a cycle length of 250 ms; reasoning the wrong way round leads to this answer.
prog-dai-013.explication: Rate is calculated as 60,000 / cycle length (in ms): 60,000 / 300 = 200 bpm. This calculation is essential because ICD detection zones are expressed in bpm or in ms depending on the manufacturer. A few reference points help: 400 ms = 150 bpm, 350 ms ≈ 171 bpm, 320 ms ≈ 188 bpm, 300 ms = 200 bpm, 260 ms ≈ 231 bpm, 240 ms = 250 bpm. The pitfall is to reason the wrong way round: the shorter the cycle length, the faster the rate.

prog-dai-014.question: According to the 2019 HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS consensus on ICD programming, what lower boundary is recommended for the slowest therapy zone in a primary prevention patient?
options: Between 140 and 150 bpm
Between 160 and 170 bpm
Between 170 and 180 bpm
Between 185 and 200 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: such a low zone encompasses exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and AF, a source of inappropriate therapies.
Incorrect: this is outdated "conventional" programming, which multiplies inappropriate therapies.
Incorrect: 170 bpm was the threshold of the conventional arm of MADIT-RIT, which was outperformed by high-rate zones.
Correct: the 2019 consensus recommends (class I) a first therapy zone between 185 and 200 bpm in primary prevention.
prog-dai-014.explication: In primary prevention patients, the consensus recommends (class I) setting the slowest therapy zone between 185 and 200 bpm. This "high-rate zone" strategy, validated notably by MADIT-RIT, greatly reduces inappropriate therapies (sinus tachycardia, AF) and unnecessary therapies for slow non-sustained VT, without increasing mortality. A zone at 140–180 bpm risks treating SVT: the conventional arm of MADIT-RIT, which treated from 170 bpm, fared worse. In secondary prevention the reasoning is different, based on the rate of the documented VT.
prog-dai-014.aRetenir: Primary prevention: first therapy zone between 185 and 200 bpm.

prog-dai-015.question: According to the 2019 programming consensus, what detection duration is recommended in primary prevention before therapy is delivered?
options: At least 2.5 seconds or 12 out of 16 intervals
At least 4 seconds or 18 out of 24 intervals
At least 6 to 12 seconds or 30 intervals
At least 60 seconds, regardless of rate
commentaires: Incorrect: this is short detection, which leads to treating many episodes that would have stopped on their own.
Incorrect: 18/24 is the "standard" detection that ADVANCE III compared with long detection, and it resulted in more therapies.
Correct: the 2019 consensus recommends (class I) at least 6 to 12 s or 30 intervals in primary prevention.
Incorrect: such a long delay for all rhythms would dangerously delay treatment of fast VT and VF.
prog-dai-015.explication: The 2019 consensus recommends (class I) prolonged detection: the tachycardia must persist for at least 6 to 12 seconds, or 30 intervals, before therapy is delivered. Many fast VTs terminate spontaneously within a few seconds: waiting avoids unnecessary ATP and shocks. MADIT-RIT and ADVANCE III (30 out of 40 intervals versus 18 out of 24) showed that this strategy reduces therapies without a significant increase in syncope. The pitfall is to believe that short detection is "safer": above all, it multiplies avoidable shocks. Conversely, a uniform one-minute delay would delay treatment of the fastest rhythms.
prog-dai-015.aRetenir: Long detection (≥ 6–12 s or 30 intervals): fewer unnecessary therapies, with no loss of safety.

prog-dai-016.question: In MADIT-RIT, compared with conventional programming, which strategies reduced inappropriate therapies, with lower all-cause mortality?
options: Therapy only from 200 bpm, or prolonged detection delays
A single low zone at 150 bpm, with ATP delivered without delay
Systematic deactivation of shocks in the VF zone in favour of ATP
A single ATP sequence in each zone, with no shocks at all
commentaires: Correct: the "high-rate" (≥ 200 bpm) and "delayed detection" arms both reduced inappropriate therapies, with lower mortality (significant in the high-rate arm).
Incorrect: this is the opposite of the MADIT-RIT strategy; a low zone and immediate therapy multiply inappropriate therapies.
Incorrect: shocks remain essential in the VF zone, where ATP is ineffective.
Incorrect: no arm withheld shocks; VF can only be treated with a shock.
prog-dai-016.explication: MADIT-RIT compared three programming strategies in 1,500 primary prevention patients. The conventional arm treated from 170 bpm after a short delay. The "high-rate" arm treated only from 200 bpm. The "delayed detection" arm imposed prolonged delays, which were longer the lower the rate. Both innovative strategies substantially reduced first inappropriate therapy. Strikingly, all-cause mortality was also significantly reduced in the high-rate arm (HR 0.45), with a reduction of similar size that did not reach significance in the delayed-detection arm (HR 0.56, p = 0.06). This is the basis of current recommendations (high-rate zones, long detection).
prog-dai-016.aRetenir: MADIT-RIT: high-rate zones or long detection = fewer inappropriate therapies; mortality significantly lower with high-rate therapy.

prog-dai-017.question: In the "delayed detection" arm (arm C) of MADIT-RIT, what delays were programmed before therapy according to ventricular rate?
options: 30 s regardless of rate, including above 250 bpm
12 s at 170–199 bpm, 60 s at 200–249 bpm, 30 s above
1 s at 170–199 bpm, 1 s at 200–249 bpm, 1 s above
60 s at 170–199 bpm, 12 s at 200–249 bpm, 2.5 s above
commentaires: Incorrect: the delays decreased stepwise, and 30 s for VF would be far too long.
Incorrect: the delays should shorten as rate increases, not the other way round.
Incorrect: this is almost immediate detection, similar to the conventional arm.
Correct: 60 s, 12 s then 2.5 s; the slower the VT, the longer one can wait.
prog-dai-017.explication: The delayed detection arm of MADIT-RIT used stepwise decreasing delays: 60 seconds from 170 to 199 bpm, 12 seconds from 200 to 249 bpm and 2.5 seconds from 250 bpm. The principle: the slower the tachycardia, the better it is tolerated and the more likely it is to stop on its own, so one can wait longer. Very fast rhythms (VF) are treated without significant delay. This detail illustrates the key idea: delayed detection reduced inappropriate therapies without an excess of syncope, with a trend towards lower mortality (HR 0.56, p = 0.06).
prog-dai-017.aRetenir: The slower the VT, the longer therapy can be delayed: this is the principle of delayed detection.

prog-dai-018.question: True or false: in ADVANCE III, long detection (30 out of 40 intervals) reduced therapies delivered compared with standard detection (18 out of 24), but at the cost of a significant increase in syncope.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the reduction in therapies (about one third) was achieved without a significant increase in syncope.
Correct: the first part is accurate, but there was no significant excess of syncope; this is what underpins the recommendation.
prog-dai-018.explication: False, because of the second part of the statement. ADVANCE III randomised about 1,900 ICD patients to standard detection of 18 out of 24 intervals or long detection of 30 out of 40 intervals. Long detection reduced therapies delivered by about one third, and lowered inappropriate shocks, without a significant increase in syncope. Together with MADIT-RIT and PainFree SST, this trial underpins the 2019 consensus recommendation for prolonged detection. The message: many fast non-sustained episodes stop on their own if given time, and waiting does not come at the price of syncope.
prog-dai-018.aRetenir: ADVANCE III: 30/40 detection = fewer therapies, same safety.

prog-dai-019.question: In a secondary prevention patient implanted for documented monomorphic VT at 165 bpm, how do you program the slowest detection zone?
prog-dai-019.reponseAttendue: About 10 bpm below the rate of the clinical VT, i.e. around 155 bpm (cycle length ≈ 385 ms), with SVT–VT discriminators enabled and ATP as first-line therapy.
prog-dai-019.explication: In secondary prevention, programming is based on the documented clinical VT: the consensus suggests setting the slowest zone about 10 bpm below the rate of that VT, so that it is detected even if it is somewhat slowed (by an antiarrhythmic drug, for example). Programming 200 bpm, as in primary prevention, would miss this patient's VT. A zone at 120 bpm would encompass exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and AF, a source of inappropriate shocks. A VF zone alone would not treat a VT at 165 bpm.
prog-dai-019.aRetenir: Secondary prevention: slowest zone ≈ 10 bpm below the documented clinical VT.

prog-dai-020.question: What distinguishes "burst" ATP from "ramp" ATP?
options: Burst keeps a constant cycle length, ramp shortens it with each pulse
Burst is a low-energy shock, ramp is a high-energy shock
Burst is reserved for the atrium, ramp is reserved for the ventricle
Burst adapts to the VT cycle length, ramp uses a fixed cycle length in ms
commentaires: Correct: burst = pulses at a constant cycle length; ramp = each pulse earlier than the previous one.
Incorrect: neither burst nor ramp is a shock; both are painless pacing.
Incorrect: both modalities are used in the ventricle for ATP of VT.
Incorrect: both are usually calculated as a percentage of the VT cycle length; the difference lies in the decrement within the sequence.
prog-dai-020.explication: ATP consists of pacing the ventricle slightly faster than the VT to penetrate the re-entrant circuit and interrupt it, painlessly. In a burst, all pulses in a sequence are delivered at the same cycle length, expressed as a percentage of the VT cycle length. In a ramp, each pulse is earlier than the previous one (decrement of a few ms per pulse), making the sequence more aggressive. Neither is a shock: both are painless pacing.
prog-dai-020.aRetenir: Burst = constant cycle length; ramp = cycle length that shortens within the sequence.

prog-dai-021.question: A VT has a cycle length of 400 ms. The first ATP is programmed as a burst at 88% of the tachycardia cycle length. What will the pacing cycle length be?
options: 312 ms
352 ms
368 ms
440 ms
commentaires: Incorrect: 312 ms corresponds to 78% of the cycle length, a more aggressive sequence.
Correct: 400 × 0.88 = 352 ms, slightly faster than the VT.
Incorrect: 368 ms corresponds to 92% of the cycle length, not 88%.
Incorrect: 440 ms is slower than the VT (110%) and would be ineffective.
prog-dai-021.explication: The burst cycle length is calculated from the measured VT cycle length: 400 × 0.88 = 352 ms, i.e. about 170 bpm for a VT at 150 bpm. Pacing slightly faster than the tachycardia makes it possible to penetrate the re-entrant circuit. 368 ms would correspond to 92%, and 440 ms would be slower than the VT and therefore ineffective. 312 ms would correspond to 78%, which is more aggressive, with a greater risk of accelerating the VT. The consensus suggests a first sequence of at least 8 pulses at about 84–88% of the VT cycle length.
prog-dai-021.aRetenir: Burst cycle length = VT cycle length × programmed percentage (e.g. 400 × 0.88 = 352 ms).

prog-dai-022.question: A VT has a cycle length of 360 ms. Ramp ATP is programmed: 8 pulses, first pulse at 81% of the VT cycle length, decrement of 10 ms per pulse. Give the cycle lengths of the first and last pulses.
prog-dai-022.reponseAttendue: First pulse ≈ 292 ms (360 × 0.81 = 291.6); each pulse is shortened by 10 ms, so the 8th pulse ≈ 292 − 70 = 222 ms (in practice limited by the programmed minimum pacing cycle length).
prog-dai-022.explication: In a ramp, the first pulse is calculated from the VT cycle length (360 × 0.81 ≈ 292 ms), then each subsequent pulse is shorter than the previous one by the programmed decrement. With 8 pulses there are 7 decrements of 10 ms, i.e. 70 ms, giving a final cycle length of around 222 ms (≈ 270 bpm). This shows that a ramp quickly becomes very aggressive, with a risk of accelerating the VT. All ICDs have a minimum ATP pacing cycle length that limits the ramp. This calculation also explains why burst is generally preferred as first-line therapy.
prog-dai-022.aRetenir: A ramp shortens by n × decrement: it quickly becomes aggressive and can accelerate the VT.

prog-dai-023.question: According to the 2015 HRS/EHRA consensus, confirmed by the 2019 update, what ATP programming is recommended in a patient with structural heart disease?
options: ATP in all VT zones up to 230 bpm, preferably as burst
No ATP above 188 bpm, shock straight away in the fast zones
Ramp ATP only, and only in the slowest VT zone
ATP reserved for secondary prevention patients with documented VT
commentaires: Correct: ATP terminates most fast monomorphic VTs; burst is as effective as ramp and less proarrhythmic.
Incorrect: withholding ATP for fast VT leads to shocks that could have been avoided.
Incorrect: burst is preferred to ramp, and ATP should cover fast VT.
Incorrect: the recommendation applies to all patients with structural heart disease, including primary prevention.
prog-dai-023.explication: In patients with structural heart disease, consensus documents recommend programming ATP in all VT zones, including for fast VT up to 230 bpm, unless ATP has proved ineffective or proarrhythmic in that patient. ATP terminates the large majority of fast monomorphic VTs, thereby avoiding a painful shock. Burst is preferred to ramp as first-line therapy: it is as effective and less proarrhythmic. On many devices, ATP can be delivered during capacitor charging, without delaying the shock if it fails.
prog-dai-023.aRetenir: ATP first, in all zones up to 230 bpm, preferably as burst.

prog-dai-024.question: As a general rule, how is the energy of the first shock in the VF zone of a transvenous ICD programmed?
options: At minimum energy (5 J), to limit the pain felt
At 50% of maximum energy, to shorten charge time
At maximum energy, unless lower energy proved effective
At 10 J above the measured defibrillation threshold
commentaires: Incorrect: an ineffective shock prolongs VF, and a lower energy does not make the shock perceptibly less painful.
Incorrect: the shorter charge time does not offset the risk of first-shock failure.
Correct: first VF shock at maximum energy (35–40 J depending on the model), unless testing has shown a lower energy to be effective.
Incorrect: defibrillation testing is no longer routine; without a measurement, maximum energy is programmed.
prog-dai-024.explication: The consensus recommends programming the first shock at the device's maximum energy (around 35 to 40 J depending on the model), unless defibrillation testing has shown a lower energy to be effective. Each ineffective shock prolongs VF and reduces the chances of success of subsequent shocks. Reducing the energy does not make the shock perceptibly less painful for the patient: any shock is felt as violent by a conscious patient. The slightly longer charge time is offset by greater efficacy. As defibrillation testing is no longer performed routinely, there is usually no measured safety margin: maximum energy is the rule.
prog-dai-024.aRetenir: First VF shock at maximum energy, unless a lower energy has proved effective.

prog-dai-025.question: According to the ICD programming consensus (2015, unchanged on this point by the 2019 update), what is the role of defibrillation testing (VF induction) at de novo implantation of a left pectoral transvenous ICD?
options: Mandatory in all patients, to confirm the safety margin
Reasonable to omit if the RV lead is well positioned with good measurements
Contraindicated in all cases since the SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD trials
To be performed only if the patient is in sinus rhythm at implantation
commentaires: Incorrect: SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD showed that omitting it is non-inferior; it is no longer routine.
Correct: class IIa for omitting it in a left pectoral implant if the fluoroscopic position and the sensing, pacing and impedance measurements are good.
Incorrect: it is not contraindicated as such and retains case-by-case indications (right-sided implantation, HCM, etc.).
Incorrect: the underlying rhythm is not the deciding criterion.
prog-dai-025.explication: The 2015 consensus (Wilkoff), which the 2019 update does not change on this point, considers it reasonable (class IIa) to omit defibrillation testing at de novo left pectoral implantation of a transvenous ICD, provided the RV lead is well positioned on fluoroscopy and the sensing, pacing and impedance measurements are good. The SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD trials showed that not testing does not impair shock efficacy during follow-up or prognosis. Testing retains case-by-case indications (right-sided implantation, generator change with an old lead, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, etc.) and was still advised in this consensus at S-ICD implantation. It is not "contraindicated" as such, but its risks (anaesthesia, complications) must be weighed up.
prog-dai-025.aRetenir: Well-positioned left pectoral transvenous ICD: defibrillation testing can be omitted.

prog-dai-026.question: What were the shared findings of the SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD trials?
options: Omitting intraoperative testing is non-inferior for shock efficacy
Intraoperative defibrillation testing reduces one-year mortality
Omitting testing increases the risk of shock failure by more than 10%
They included only patients with a subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD)
commentaires: Correct: in both trials, omitting testing impaired neither the efficacy of shocks for spontaneous arrhythmias nor clinical outcomes.
Incorrect: no mortality benefit was shown with routine testing.
Incorrect: omitting testing did not increase shock failures.
Incorrect: both trials involved transvenous ICDs.
prog-dai-026.explication: SIMPLE (about 2,500 patients) and NORDIC ICD (about 1,000 patients) randomised patients receiving a transvenous ICD to undergo or not undergo intraoperative defibrillation testing. In both trials, omitting testing was non-inferior: no impairment of shock efficacy for spontaneous arrhythmias or of clinical outcomes (arrhythmic death or shock failure). On the strength of these results, the 2015 consensus (Wilkoff), unchanged on this point by the 2019 focused update, considers omission of testing reasonable (class IIa) at a standard de novo left pectoral implantation. They did not concern the S-ICD, for which this consensus still advised testing.
prog-dai-026.aRetenir: SIMPLE and NORDIC ICD: no demonstrated benefit of routine defibrillation testing.

prog-dai-027.question: Defibrillation testing fails at maximum energy during implantation of a transvenous ICD. Which measures may improve defibrillation efficacy?
options: Reversing shock polarity
Repositioning the RV lead (more apical or septal as appropriate)
Changing the shock vector (adding or removing the SVC coil)
Increasing the number of ATP pulses
Giving IV amiodarone to lower the defibrillation threshold
commentaires: Correct: the efficacy of a biphasic waveform depends on polarity in some patients.
Correct: a different lead position alters the distribution of the electrical field.
Correct: changing the vector (SVC coil, active can or not) can lower the threshold.
Incorrect: ATP does not treat the VF induced during testing.
Incorrect: amiodarone, on the contrary, tends to raise the defibrillation threshold; this must be taken into account, not added.
prog-dai-027.explication: When the defibrillation threshold is high, several levers are available. Polarity can be reversed, because the efficacy of a biphasic waveform depends on polarity in some patients. The shock vector can be changed (SVC coil, active can or not) or the RV lead repositioned. In refractory cases, an additional coil or a subcutaneous array can be added. Amiodarone can raise the defibrillation threshold: this must be taken into account in current medication, and it should certainly not be given to lower the threshold. Increasing the number of ATP pulses changes nothing: ATP does not treat the VF induced during testing.
prog-dai-027.aRetenir: High defibrillation threshold: polarity, vector, lead position and medication review (amiodarone) before resorting to additional hardware.

prog-dai-028.question: What is the principle behind the "onset" (sudden onset) discrimination criterion?
options: VT is irregular, whereas SVT is perfectly regular
VT has more atrial than ventricular complexes
The tachycardia QRS is compared with a sinus rhythm template
VT starts abruptly, whereas sinus tachycardia builds up gradually
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the idea behind the stability criterion (and it is the wrong way round: monomorphic VT tends to be regular).
Incorrect: this is the A/V relationship; VT actually gives V > A.
Incorrect: this is the principle of the morphology criterion.
Correct: onset analyses the transition, abrupt in VT and gradual in sinus tachycardia.
prog-dai-028.explication: The onset criterion analyses the transition into the tachycardia: abrupt shortening of cycle length suggests VT, whereas gradual acceleration suggests sinus tachycardia. It is assessed only at the start of the episode. It is not used to judge regularity (that is stability) or morphology (which compares the QRS with a sinus rhythm template). Its main limitation: some SVTs (atrial tachycardia, AVNRT) also start abruptly.
prog-dai-028.aRetenir: Onset: abrupt start = VT; gradual acceleration = sinus tachycardia.

prog-dai-029.question: Which discrimination criterion is most useful for distinguishing rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation from monomorphic VT in a single-chamber ICD?
options: The A/V relationship
Onset (suddenness)
Cycle length stability
Pacing threshold
commentaires: Incorrect: the A/V relationship requires an atrial lead, which a single-chamber ICD lacks.
Incorrect: AF starts as abruptly as VT; onset discriminates it poorly.
Correct: conducted AF gives irregular ventricular cycles, monomorphic VT regular cycles.
Incorrect: this is not an SVT–VT discrimination criterion.
prog-dai-029.explication: Conducted AF gives irregular ventricular cycles, whereas monomorphic VT is usually regular: this is the principle of the stability criterion. It is less reliable at very fast rates, where AF may appear "pseudo-regular", and in the presence of antiarrhythmic drugs, which make some VTs irregular. Onset discriminates AF poorly, as its start is as abrupt as that of VT. The A/V relationship requires an atrial lead, which is absent in a single-chamber device.
prog-dai-029.aRetenir: Stability = the discriminator of choice for AF (irregular) versus VT (regular).

prog-dai-030.question: Which situation is most likely to cause an error by the morphology criterion (comparison with the sinus rhythm QRS template)?
options: VF at more than 250 bpm, in the VF zone
Monomorphic VT whose QRS differs markedly from the stored template
SVT with rate-related functional bundle branch block
Sinus tachycardia with narrow QRS complexes identical to the template
commentaires: Incorrect: in the VF zone, discriminators do not usually apply.
Incorrect: a VT that differs markedly from the template is precisely the one that is well recognised.
Correct: aberrancy makes the QRS differ from the template and leads to a false diagnosis of VT.
Incorrect: a QRS identical to the template is correctly classified as SVT.
prog-dai-030.explication: The morphology criterion compares each tachycardia QRS with a template recorded during intrinsic rhythm. If the SVT is accompanied by aberrant conduction (rate-related functional bundle branch block), the QRS complexes differ from the template and the device wrongly concludes that it is VT, with a risk of inappropriate therapy. Other sources of error are an outdated template (QRS changes over time or with drugs) and signal saturation (clipping). A VT that differs markedly from the template is, on the contrary, well recognised. In the VF zone, discriminators do not usually apply.
prog-dai-030.aRetenir: Morphology: beware of rate-related aberrancy and outdated templates.

prog-dai-031.question: A dual-chamber ICD records a regular tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 190 bpm and a dissociated atrial rate of 95 bpm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
AVNRT
Sinus tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
commentaires: Incorrect: flutter with 2:1 conduction gives A > V (A twice as fast as V).
Incorrect: AVNRT gives A = V, as both chambers are activated together.
Incorrect: sinus tachycardia gives A = V, as each P wave is conducted.
Correct: V > A with dissociation = VT until proven otherwise, after checking atrial sensing.
prog-dai-031.explication: When the ventricular rate exceeds the atrial rate (V > A), the diagnosis of VT is almost certain: this is the most robust criterion in dual-chamber algorithms. Sinus tachycardia, AVNRT and flutter with 2:1 conduction, on the contrary, give A = V or A > V. The pitfall is atrial undersensing (low-amplitude P waves, atrial blanking or refractory periods), which can wrongly suggest V > A: the electrograms must always be reviewed.
prog-dai-031.aRetenir: V > A = VT until proven otherwise (after checking atrial sensing).

prog-dai-032.question: True or false: the onset criterion can wrongly delay treatment of a VT that starts during exercise-induced sinus tachycardia.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: during fast sinus tachycardia, the transition to VT may occur without abrupt cycle length shortening, and therapy is withheld.
Incorrect: this is a well-known limitation of onset, hence its combination with other criteria and with a time-out.
prog-dai-032.explication: True: if VT occurs while the patient is already in fast sinus tachycardia, the transition to VT may occur without abrupt cycle length shortening. The device may then consider the episode to be sinus and withhold therapy. This is why onset is often combined with other criteria (morphology, A/V relationship). Some devices also allow a time-out, after which therapy is delivered even if the criteria suggest SVT. In return, this time-out exposes the patient to inappropriate shocks during prolonged SVT, so it must be programmed judiciously.
prog-dai-032.aRetenir: Onset: risk of missing a VT that starts during sinus tachycardia.

prog-dai-033.question: According to the 2015 HRS/EHRA consensus on ICD programming, up to what rate should SVT–VT discriminators remain active?
options: Up to 150 bpm; above this, therapy should be immediate
Up to 170 bpm, the upper limit of sinus tachycardia
Up to at least 200 bpm, and possibly up to 230 bpm
Only in the VF zone, to avoid shocks for SVT
commentaires: Incorrect: many conducted AF or flutter episodes exceed 150 bpm; they would be shocked without analysis.
Incorrect: fast SVTs, especially in young patients, frequently exceed 170 bpm.
Correct: the 2015 consensus (class I) recommends discriminators above 200 bpm, potentially up to 230 bpm.
Incorrect: at VF rates, discriminators precisely do not apply, so as not to delay treatment.
prog-dai-033.explication: Fast SVTs, in particular conducted AF and flutter in young patients, can exceed 200 bpm. The 2015 consensus (class I) therefore recommends programming discriminators for rhythms above 200 bpm and potentially up to 230 bpm, unless contraindicated in the individual patient. Limiting discriminators to the slowest zone lets fast SVTs enter a zone where they are shocked without analysis. Conversely, at VF rates, discriminators do not apply so as not to delay treatment.
prog-dai-033.aRetenir: Discriminators active up to 200 or even 230 bpm to avoid shocking fast SVTs.

prog-dai-034.question: Which of the following situations can cause an inappropriate shock in an ICD recipient?
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Exercise-induced sinus tachycardia exceeding the therapy zone
Normal use of a mobile phone held to the opposite ear
Noise from a fractured lead
Sustained monomorphic VT at 220 bpm
commentaires: Correct: rapid AF is the leading cause of inappropriate shocks.
Correct: sinus tachycardia entering the therapy zone may be shocked.
Incorrect: a mobile phone in normal use does not interfere with the ICD.
Correct: lead noise is counted as very short cycles and can trigger a shock.
Incorrect: a shock for sustained VT at 220 bpm is appropriate.
prog-dai-034.explication: Supraventricular tachycardias, first and foremost AF with rapid ventricular response, followed by sinus tachycardia, are the leading cause of inappropriate shocks. Next come oversensing: T waves, lead noise (conductor fracture, insulation breach), electromagnetic interference and myopotentials. Mobile phones in normal use cause no problems; patients are simply advised not to keep them over the device. Prevention relies on appropriate programming and on AF control (beta-blockers, ablation). A shock for sustained VT at 220 bpm, however, is an appropriate shock, even if ATP might sometimes have avoided it.
prog-dai-034.aRetenir: Inappropriate shocks: SVT first (mainly AF), then oversensing.

prog-dai-035.question: Which measures reduce the risk of inappropriate shocks in an ICD recipient?
options: Programming high-rate therapy zones and prolonged detection
Disabling discriminators above 170 bpm so as not to delay shocks
Enabling lead integrity alerts and remote monitoring
Controlling the ventricular rate in AF (beta-blocker, ablation if needed)
Lowering the first therapy zone to 150 bpm
commentaires: Correct: high-rate zones and long detection allow episodes to terminate on their own (MADIT-RIT, ADVANCE III).
Incorrect: on the contrary, discriminators should remain active up to 200 or even 230 bpm to recognise fast SVTs.
Correct: they make it possible to act on lead noise before it triggers a shock.
Correct: rapid AF is the leading cause of inappropriate shocks.
Incorrect: exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and AF would easily enter the zone.
prog-dai-035.explication: Preventing inappropriate shocks combines programming and medical management. High-rate zones and long detection allow fast episodes to terminate on their own (MADIT-RIT, ADVANCE III). Discriminators, kept active up to 200 or even 230 bpm, make it possible to recognise fast SVTs: disabling them from 170 bpm would result in these SVTs being shocked without analysis. Lead integrity alerts and remote monitoring make it possible to intervene before a shock occurs in the event of lead noise. Controlling AF removes the leading cause. Lowering the zone to 150 bpm does the opposite: exercise-induced sinus tachycardia and AF easily enter it.
prog-dai-035.aRetenir: High-rate zones, long detection, discriminators, lead alerts and AF control.

prog-dai-036.question: By what mechanism can T-wave oversensing cause an inappropriate shock?
options: It blocks capacitor charging for the whole duration of the episode
It triggers inappropriate rapid atrial pacing
It reduces the energy actually delivered by the shock
Each cycle is counted twice, so the measured rate doubles
commentaires: Incorrect: oversensing does not prevent charging; it is precisely what triggers it.
Incorrect: the problem concerns ventricular sensing, not atrial pacing.
Incorrect: shock energy is not altered by sensing.
Correct: the QRS and then the T wave are counted; a sinus rate of 100 bpm becomes a measured 200 bpm, within the therapy zone.
prog-dai-036.explication: When the T wave is sensed as a QRS, each beat is counted twice. A sinus rhythm at 100 bpm is thus measured at 200 bpm, within the therapy zone, which may lead to inappropriate ATP or a shock. On the electrogram, markers alternate between the QRS and the T wave, with alternating short and long intervals. This phenomenon is favoured by a low-amplitude QRS or a large T wave.
prog-dai-036.aRetenir: T-wave oversensing = double counting = measured rate doubled.

prog-dai-037.question: Regarding T-wave oversensing in a transvenous ICD, which statements are correct?
options: Hypokalaemia promotes it by increasing T-wave amplitude
A low-amplitude R wave promotes it
Decreasing sensitivity (increasing the mV value) may correct it, at the risk of VF undersensing
T-wave rejection algorithms available on some devices can help
It is never seen except with the subcutaneous ICD
commentaires: Incorrect: it is hyperkalaemia that increases the T wave; hypokalaemia flattens it.
Correct: a small QRS brings its amplitude closer to that of the T wave.
Correct: this is possible, but it must be ensured that low-amplitude VF is still sensed.
Correct: some manufacturers offer dedicated T-wave rejection algorithms.
Incorrect: it is more common with the S-ICD, but also occurs with transvenous ICDs.
prog-dai-037.explication: T-wave oversensing is favoured by anything that increases the T wave (hyperkalaemia, long QT syndrome, some cardiomyopathies) or reduces the R wave (lead in a scar area, maturation of the lead–myocardium interface). Hypokalaemia, by contrast, flattens the T wave and brings out U waves. Making sensing less sensitive can solve the problem, but as the ICD must sense low-amplitude VF, any reduction in sensitivity requires confirmation that VF will still be sensed. Some manufacturers offer dedicated T-wave rejection algorithms, and lead repositioning is sometimes still necessary. The phenomenon is more common with the S-ICD, but it also occurs with transvenous ICDs.
prog-dai-037.aRetenir: T-wave oversensing: look for the cause (potassium, low R wave) and never sacrifice VF sensing.

prog-dai-038.question: At ICD interrogation, which appearance is most suggestive of noise due to lead fracture?
options: Regular intervals at 350 ms, EGMs identical to those in sinus rhythm
Gradual fall in battery voltage over several months of follow-up
Atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate
Non-physiological intervals on near-field, absent on far-field
commentaires: Incorrect: a regular rhythm with sinus EGMs suggests sinus tachycardia or SVT, not noise.
Incorrect: this is normal battery depletion, unrelated to lead integrity.
Incorrect: A > V points to SVT (flutter, atrial tachycardia), not lead noise.
Correct: noise produces intervals too short to be physiological, absent from the far-field channel, which shows the true rhythm.
prog-dai-038.explication: Lead noise (conductor fracture, insulation breach, faulty connection) produces high-frequency, irregular and intermittent signals, generating intervals far too short to be physiological. It appears on the sensing channel (near-field) but not on the far-field channel (can–coil), which shows the normal underlying rhythm. Noise is often provoked by arm movements or posture. Pacing impedance may be abnormal (very high in the event of fracture) but may also remain normal between episodes. A regular rhythm at 350 ms with sinus EGMs suggests sinus tachycardia or SVT, not noise.
prog-dai-038.aRetenir: Lead noise: non-physiological intervals, on the near-field EGM only, often positional.

prog-dai-039.question: An ICD recipient has received 3 shocks in one hour. Interrogation shows intermittent noise on the RV lead, an underlying sinus rhythm and a very high pacing impedance. What is the priority?
options: Suspend therapies under ECG monitoring, then arrange lead revision
Extend detection and send the patient home under surveillance
Increase shock energy to ensure first-shock efficacy
Start amiodarone and arrange a remote ICD check
commentaires: Correct: inappropriate shocks due to probable fracture; therapies are suspended (programmer or magnet) under ECG monitoring, with an external defibrillator at hand.
Incorrect: extending detection does not abolish the noise; the patient remains exposed to repeated shocks.
Incorrect: the shocks are inappropriate; their energy is not the problem.
Incorrect: there is no arrhythmia to treat; the underlying rhythm is sinus.
prog-dai-039.explication: These are inappropriate shocks due to probable RV lead fracture: the immediate risk is repeated painful shocks, or even induction of a genuine arrhythmia. Therapies are therefore suspended (programmer, or magnet if no programmer is available), under continuous ECG monitoring with an external defibrillator available, since the patient is no longer protected. Pacing is also checked if the patient is pacemaker-dependent. The lead must then be replaced or supplemented. Extending detection does not abolish the noise, and amiodarone or a higher energy make no sense here.
prog-dai-039.aRetenir: Shocks due to lead noise: suspend therapies under ECG monitoring, then revise the lead.

prog-dai-040.question: List at least four findings at ICD interrogation that point to a defibrillation lead fracture.
prog-dai-040.reponseAttendue: Very short, non-physiological intervals (short-interval counters), intermittent noise on the near-field EGM that is absent from the far-field, an abrupt change or abnormal value of pacing and/or shock impedance, repeated "fast" non-sustained episodes, noise reproduced by manoeuvres (arm movements, posture), a triggered lead integrity alert.
prog-dai-040.explication: The diagnosis of lead fracture rests on a body of evidence, as no single finding is perfect on its own. Counters of non-physiological short intervals and numerous very fast non-sustained episodes are early signs. Pacing or shock impedance may change abruptly (often rising in the case of conductor fracture), but may remain normal when the fracture is intermittent. Comparing near-field and far-field is key: the noise is absent from the far-field. Provocative manoeuvres (arm movements, deep breathing) often reproduce the noise. Lead integrity alerts, which should always be enabled, combine these parameters.
prog-dai-040.aRetenir: Lead fracture: non-physiological intervals, noise on the near-field only, abnormal impedance, provoked noise.

prog-dai-041.question: What most commonly happens when a magnet is placed over an ICD?
options: The ICD immediately delivers a test shock
The ICD switches to asynchronous pacing at 100 bpm
Therapies are suspended for as long as the magnet is in place
The ICD is permanently deactivated, even after the magnet is removed
commentaires: Incorrect: a magnet never triggers a shock.
Incorrect: that is the response of a pacemaker; in an ICD, pacing generally remains unchanged.
Correct: ATP and shocks are suspended while the magnet is applied and resume when it is removed; bradycardia pacing is unchanged.
Incorrect: the effect is transient in most current ICDs; therapies resume when the magnet is removed.
prog-dai-041.explication: In most ICDs, a magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia detection and therapy for as long as it is held over the device; therapies resume when it is removed. Unlike in a pacemaker, a magnet does not generally switch bradycardia pacing to an asynchronous mode in an ICD. This is useful in emergencies (inappropriate shocks, electrosurgery, end of life). The magnet response may be programmable depending on the manufacturer, hence the importance of checking the device as soon as possible.
prog-dai-041.aRetenir: Magnet over an ICD: therapies suspended while it is in place, pacing unchanged (in general).

prog-dai-042.question: An ICD recipient receives a single shock. Afterwards they feel well, with no chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Contact the device clinic or send a transmission, review within 24–48 h
Call the emergency services immediately for transfer to the emergency department
Do nothing: a single well-tolerated shock has no consequences
Stop their beta-blocker until the next clinic appointment
commentaires: Correct: the episode must be reviewed promptly, but it is not a life-threatening emergency.
Incorrect: a single shock followed by good clinical status does not warrant an emergency call (overreaction).
Incorrect: every shock must be analysed (appropriate or not, trigger) and carries prognostic value.
Incorrect: medical therapy should never be stopped on the patient's own initiative.
prog-dai-042.explication: A single shock followed by good clinical status does not warrant an emergency call. The device clinic should, however, be contacted (or a manual remote monitoring transmission sent) to review the episode: appropriate or inappropriate shock, trigger, adjustment of treatment or programming. Doing nothing would be a mistake: shocks, whether appropriate or not, are associated with a worse prognosis and should prompt a search for a cause. Medical therapy should never be stopped on the patient's own initiative.
prog-dai-042.aRetenir: Single well-tolerated shock: not an emergency, but contact the device clinic for prompt review.

prog-dai-043.question: In which situations should an ICD recipient call the emergency services immediately?
options: Several shocks in quick succession
A shock followed by chest pain
A shock followed by loss of consciousness
A single shock followed by good clinical status
An audible battery end-of-life alert
commentaires: Correct: several shocks in quick succession raise concern about electrical storm or a series of inappropriate shocks.
Correct: a shock followed by chest pain requires immediate care.
Correct: a shock followed by loss of consciousness requires an emergency call.
Incorrect: a single well-tolerated shock warrants prompt contact with the device clinic, not the emergency services.
Incorrect: a battery end-of-life alert warrants contact with the device clinic, not an emergency call.
prog-dai-043.explication: Several shocks in quick succession raise concern about electrical storm or a series of inappropriate shocks (lead noise, rapid AF), both of which are emergencies. A shock followed by symptoms (chest pain, loss of consciousness, dyspnoea, confusion) also requires immediate medical care. A single well-tolerated shock calls for prompt but non-urgent contact with the device clinic. An audible battery end-of-life alert warrants prompt contact with the device clinic, not an emergency call.
prog-dai-043.aRetenir: Multiple shocks or a shock with symptoms = call the emergency services.

prog-dai-044.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, how is electrical storm defined in an ICD recipient?
prog-dai-044.reponseAttendue: At least 3 episodes of sustained VT or VF, or of appropriate ICD therapies (ATP or shocks), within a 24-hour period.
prog-dai-044.explication: Electrical storm is defined as at least three episodes of sustained VT or VF (or of appropriate therapies, ATP or shocks) within 24 hours. It is an emergency requiring sedation, a beta-blocker and an antiarrhythmic drug, identification and correction of triggers (ischaemia, potassium disturbance, decompensation), and early consideration of ablation. Inappropriate shocks, even if repeated, do not define electrical storm, which concerns genuine ventricular arrhythmias. Frequent PVCs are not enough.
prog-dai-044.aRetenir: Electrical storm = ≥ 3 sustained VT/VF episodes or appropriate therapies within 24 h.

prog-dai-045.question: A patient attends clinic after a single, well-tolerated shock. What are the main steps in your management?
prog-dai-045.reponseAttendue: Clinical examination and ECG; ICD interrogation to classify the shock (appropriate: VT/VF; inappropriate: SVT, oversensing, lead noise) and check lead measurements; search for triggers (ischaemia, electrolytes/potassium, heart failure decompensation, adherence, drugs, thyroid dysfunction); then adjustment of treatment (beta-blocker, antiarrhythmic drug, VT or AF ablation) and/or programming (ATP, zones, discriminators); information and support for the patient.
prog-dai-045.explication: After a shock, the first question is whether it was appropriate: analysis of the stored electrograms answers this. If it was appropriate, look for a contributing cause (ischaemia, hypokalaemia, decompensation, poor adherence) and optimise treatment, or even consider ablation if episodes recur. If it was inappropriate, correct the cause (AF control, reprogramming, lead revision if there is noise). Also check that ATP is properly programmed, as some shocks could have been avoided. Finally, the psychological impact of shocks is real and must be addressed.
prog-dai-045.aRetenir: After a shock: interrogate the device to find out whether it was appropriate, find the cause, adjust treatment and programming.

prog-dai-046.question: What do the SCD-HeFT data (analysis by Poole et al., 2008) show about the prognosis of patients who have received an ICD shock?
options: Only inappropriate shocks are associated with increased mortality
Appropriate shocks improve prognosis by "conditioning" the myocardium
Shocks have no prognostic value once the arrhythmia has been treated
Both appropriate and inappropriate shocks are linked to higher mortality
commentaires: Incorrect: the risk of death was increased mainly after an appropriate shock.
Incorrect: no data suggest a beneficial effect of shocks; if anything, they are harmful.
Incorrect: shocks, appropriate or not, were associated with increased subsequent mortality.
Correct: the association is clear after an appropriate shock and more modest, but present, after an inappropriate shock.
prog-dai-046.explication: In the analysis by Poole et al., patients who received an appropriate shock had a markedly increased risk of death, and inappropriate shocks remained associated with increased mortality, although more modestly. This is an association: a shock is mainly a marker of more advanced heart disease, but it may also have a harmful effect of its own. These data, together with MADIT-RIT, reinforced the goal of limiting all avoidable shocks. They also justify reassessing heart failure after a shock.
prog-dai-046.aRetenir: Every shock, appropriate or not, is a prognostic warning sign.

prog-dai-047.question: True or false: deactivating ICD shocks at the request of a patient at the end of life is an ethically and legally accepted practice, distinct from euthanasia.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: it is a refusal of treatment, recognised by the 2010 HRS/EHRA consensus documents and, in France, by the Claeys-Leonetti law.
Incorrect: deactivating shocks allows the underlying disease to take its course, without any act that causes death; it is not euthanasia.
prog-dai-047.explication: True: the 2010 HRS and EHRA consensus documents consider that any patient (or their representative) may request withdrawal of a therapy, including ICD shocks. This is a refusal of treatment, which allows the underlying disease to take its course, not an act that causes death. In France, the Claeys-Leonetti law also recognises the right to refuse treatment. Ideally, the issue is raised at implantation and then at major changes in health status, as recommended by the 2022 ESC guidelines. The decision is documented in the medical record.
prog-dai-047.aRetenir: Deactivating shocks at the end of life = respecting refusal of treatment, not euthanasia.

prog-dai-048.question: A pacing-dependent ICD recipient receiving palliative care asks that no further attempts be made to "resuscitate" him. What approach is usually proposed?
options: Deactivate shocks and ATP while keeping pacing on
Explant the device to respect the patient's wishes
Deactivate all pacing at the same time as the shocks
Change nothing, as deactivation is prohibited in France
commentaires: Correct: this is the usual approach, after discussion with the patient and the team, with a documented and reversible decision.
Incorrect: explantation exposes the patient to an unnecessary procedure and has no justification.
Incorrect: in a dependent patient, stopping pacing could cause immediate death; pacing causes no discomfort.
Incorrect: refusal of treatment is a recognised right; deactivation is legal.
prog-dai-048.explication: At the end of life, shocks are painful and futile: their deactivation is the most common request. Bradycardia pacing causes no discomfort, and stopping it in a dependent patient could cause immediate death. Most teams therefore keep it on, although consensus documents also recognise the right to refuse pacing after in-depth discussion. Explantation has no justification. The decision is multidisciplinary and documented, and the patient can reverse it. If no programmer is available, a magnet can suspend shocks in an emergency.
prog-dai-048.aRetenir: End of life: deactivate shocks, generally keep pacing on.

prog-dai-049.question: According to the 2022 ESC guidelines, when should ICD deactivation be discussed with the patient?
options: From implantation, then at each turning point in the disease
Never: the decision rests with the doctor alone, to spare the patient
Only in the terminal phase, so as not to worry the patient
Only at generator replacement, at battery end of life
commentaires: Correct: the 2022 ESC guidelines recommend discussing it from implantation and then at each turning point in the disease.
Incorrect: the process is shared; decisions are not made without the patient.
Incorrect: waiting until the terminal phase leads to painful shocks through lack of planning, or to a decision made without the patient.
Incorrect: generator replacement is a good time to revisit the issue, but not the only one.
prog-dai-049.explication: The 2022 ESC guidelines recommend informing the patient and discussing ICD deactivation before implantation and then at each turning point in the disease (worsening heart failure, advanced cancer, transition to palliative care). Waiting until the terminal phase often leads to painful shocks at the end of life through lack of planning, or to a decision made without the patient. Generator replacement is also a good time to reassess the indication, but not the only one. The process is shared: decisions are not made without the patient.
prog-dai-049.aRetenir: Discuss deactivation from implantation onwards, then at each turning point in the disease.

prog-dai-050.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, which profile corresponds to a class I (level A) indication for CRT?
options: Sinus rhythm, LVEF 45%, QRS 110 ms, NYHA III
LVEF ≤ 35%, QRS 120 ms, marked echocardiographic dyssynchrony
Normal LVEF, isolated RBBB with QRS 140 ms
Sinus rhythm, LVEF ≤ 35%, LBBB 150 ms, symptomatic
commentaires: Incorrect: LVEF > 35% and narrow QRS, no indication for CRT.
Incorrect: QRS < 130 ms = no CRT, even with echocardiographic dyssynchrony (EchoCRT).
Incorrect: normal LVEF and isolated RBBB do not warrant CRT.
Correct: this is the only class IA indication, provided medical therapy is optimal.
prog-dai-050.explication: The strongest indication for CRT, and the only class IA one, combines sinus rhythm, symptomatic heart failure despite optimal therapy, LVEF ≤ 35% and QRS ≥ 150 ms with LBBB morphology. This is the population that benefited most in the major trials (CARE-HF, COMPANION, MADIT-CRT). The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines restate this indication unchanged (class I, level A). They add that, in this profile, medical therapy may be started and CRT planned at the same time (class IIb), with LVEF reassessed before implantation. A QRS < 130 ms is not an indication, even with echocardiographic dyssynchrony (EchoCRT). An LVEF of 45%, a normal LVEF or isolated RBBB do not warrant CRT.
prog-dai-050.aRetenir: CRT class I (ESC 2021 and 2026): LVEF ≤ 35%, LBBB, QRS ≥ 150 ms, symptomatic on optimal therapy.

prog-dai-051.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, what is the class of recommendation for CRT in a symptomatic patient in sinus rhythm with LVEF ≤ 35% and a QRS of 140 ms without LBBB morphology?
options: Class I
Class IIa
Class IIb
Class III
commentaires: Incorrect: class I is reserved for LBBB ≥ 150 ms.
Incorrect: IIa applies to LBBB 130–149 ms and non-LBBB ≥ 150 ms.
Correct: non-LBBB between 130 and 149 ms = class IIb, where the benefit is least certain.
Incorrect: class III applies to QRS < 130 ms (unless ventricular pacing is needed).
prog-dai-051.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines grade the indication according to QRS duration and morphology. LBBB ≥ 150 ms: class I. LBBB 130–149 ms: IIa. Non-LBBB ≥ 150 ms: IIa. Non-LBBB 130–149 ms: IIb, because the benefit is least certain. Below 130 ms, CRT is not indicated (class III), unless ventricular pacing is needed for high-grade AV block. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines keep exactly the same grading, still with LVEF ≤ 35%, but with level of evidence C for the three intermediate indications. The pitfall is to apply the LBBB thresholds to non-LBBB.
prog-dai-051.aRetenir: Non-LBBB 130–149 ms = CRT class IIb only (ESC 2021 and 2026).

prog-dai-052.question: True or false: in a heart failure patient with LVEF ≤ 35% and QRS < 130 ms, CRT is indicated if echocardiography shows mechanical dyssynchrony.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: EchoCRT was stopped for futility, with excess mortality in the CRT arm in these narrow-QRS patients.
Correct: QRS < 130 ms = CRT not recommended (class III), regardless of echocardiographic dyssynchrony.
prog-dai-052.explication: False: the EchoCRT trial tested CRT in patients with a narrow QRS (< 130 ms) selected on the basis of echocardiographic dyssynchrony. It was stopped for futility, with significant excess mortality in the CRT arm. The 2021 ESC guidelines therefore advise against CRT if the QRS is < 130 ms (class III), unless the patient has another indication for ventricular pacing. Echocardiographic dyssynchrony is not a validated selection criterion.
prog-dai-052.aRetenir: QRS < 130 ms: no CRT, even with echocardiographic dyssynchrony (EchoCRT).

prog-dai-053.question: What percentage of biventricular pacing is targeted in a CRT patient?
options: More than 80%
More than 90%
More than 95%
More than 98%
commentaires: Incorrect: 80% leaves one beat in five unresynchronised, with a markedly smaller benefit.
Incorrect: 90% seems high but is still associated with a poorer outcome.
Incorrect: even 95% falls short of the target associated with the greatest survival benefit.
Correct: the greatest mortality reduction is achieved above 98% (Hayes et al.).
prog-dai-053.explication: CRT is effective only if biventricular pacing is almost continuous. The analysis by Hayes et al. (more than 36,000 remotely monitored patients) showed that the greatest reduction in mortality was achieved with more than 98% biventricular pacing. Even a percentage of 90 to 95%, which seems high, is associated with a poorer outcome. Any lower percentage should prompt a search for a cause: AF, PVCs, an excessively long AV delay, loss of LV capture.
prog-dai-053.aRetenir: CRT target: more than 98% biventricular pacing.

prog-dai-054.question: Which causes may explain a fall in the percentage of biventricular pacing in a CRT patient?
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid AV conduction
Frequent PVCs
Programmed AV delay longer than the intrinsic PR interval
Programmed AV delay much shorter than the intrinsic PR interval
Atrial pacing at 60 bpm
commentaires: Correct: rapid AF conducts spontaneously to the ventricles and bypasses pacing.
Correct: these are unresynchronised beats, which can also place the next P wave within the PVARP.
Correct: the native QRS occurs before pacing, which is inhibited.
Incorrect: a short AV delay, on the contrary, promotes biventricular capture.
Incorrect: atrial pacing does not prevent synchronised ventricular pacing afterwards.
prog-dai-054.explication: Biventricular pacing is lost as soon as intrinsic conduction "wins" over pacing. Rapid AF conducts spontaneously to the ventricles. Frequent PVCs are unresynchronised beats and can also place the next P wave within the PVARP. An AV delay longer than the intrinsic PR interval allows the native QRS to occur before pacing; a short AV delay, on the contrary, promotes biventricular capture. Another classic cause is a sinus rate above the maximum tracking rate, leading to Wenckebach-type behaviour and then 2:1 block with intrinsic conduction. Atrial pacing at 60 bpm, by contrast, does not prevent synchronised ventricular pacing afterwards.
prog-dai-054.aRetenir: Fall in % BiV pacing: think of AF, PVCs, an excessively long AV delay and an excessively fast sinus rate.

prog-dai-055.question: A CRT patient is in permanent AF with only 85% biventricular pacing despite optimised rate-control therapy. What do the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend?
options: Stop CRT, which has become useless in permanent AF
Program a longer AV delay to promote capture
Consider atrioventricular junction ablation
Switch to AAI mode to preserve native conduction
commentaires: Incorrect: CRT remains beneficial in AF if biventricular pacing is near-complete.
Incorrect: the AV delay is meaningless in AF, with no organised atrial activity to track.
Correct: the 2021 ESC guidelines (IIa) propose AV junction ablation to achieve biventricular pacing close to 100%.
Incorrect: AAI mode is impossible in AF.
prog-dai-055.explication: In AF, intrinsic AV conduction competes with biventricular pacing. When rate-control therapy is insufficient, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering AV junction ablation (class IIa) to ensure complete biventricular pacing. The AV delay is meaningless in AF, as there is no organised atrial activity to track. AAI mode is impossible in AF. Beware also of fusion or pseudo-fusion beats, which artificially inflate the pacing counter.
prog-dai-055.aRetenir: CRT + AF with incomplete BiV pacing: consider AV junction ablation.

prog-dai-056.question: A young CRT patient loses biventricular pacing on exertion: the trends show a sinus rate of 135 bpm with a programmed maximum tracking rate of 120 bpm. What is the most logical measure?
options: Raise the maximum tracking rate, together with a beta-blocker
Lower the maximum tracking rate to 100 bpm for safety
Extend the AV delay to allow intrinsic conduction through
Program VVI mode to override the sinus rate
commentaires: Correct: raise the maximum tracking rate (checking that the total atrial refractory period allows it) and optimise the beta-blocker.
Incorrect: lowering this rate would worsen the loss of pacing on exertion.
Incorrect: extending the AV delay would promote unresynchronised intrinsic conduction.
Incorrect: VVI mode would abolish AV synchrony.
prog-dai-056.explication: When the sinus rate exceeds the maximum tracking rate, the device can no longer track every P wave: Wenckebach-type behaviour, then 2:1 block. In a patient with preserved AV conduction, the intrinsic (unresynchronised) QRS takes over, precisely on exertion. The maximum tracking rate is therefore raised, making sure that the total atrial refractory period allows it, and the beta-blocker is optimised. Lowering this rate would make the situation worse. Extending the AV delay would promote intrinsic conduction, and VVI mode would abolish AV synchrony.
prog-dai-056.aRetenir: CRT: maximum tracking rate high enough to cover the exercise sinus rate.

prog-dai-057.question: On the 12-lead ECG of a CRT patient, which appearance should raise suspicion of loss of LV capture with RV-only pacing?
options: Paced QRS with dominant R in V1 and Q wave in lead I
Narrow QRS with no visible spike, identical to the intrinsic QRS
Paced QRS with QS or rS in V1 and broad R in lead I
Retrograde P wave after each paced QRS
commentaires: Incorrect: this is the usual appearance of effective biventricular pacing (LV contribution).
Incorrect: a narrow QRS with no spike reflects intrinsic conduction, not RV-only pacing.
Correct: RV-only pacing activates from right to left, with a left-sided delay pattern: QS in V1, R in lead I.
Incorrect: a retrograde P wave gives no information about LV capture.
prog-dai-057.explication: With RV-only pacing (from the apex or septum), activation proceeds from right to left, giving an LBBB-like pattern with a QS complex in V1 and a positive R wave in lead I. With effective biventricular pacing, the LV contribution usually produces an R wave in V1 and a Q wave (or a negative pattern) in lead I. These criteria are not absolute (lead positions, scars), hence the value of comparison with the reference ECG recorded after implantation. Loss of LV capture is confirmed with the programmer by an LV threshold test.
prog-dai-057.aRetenir: RV-only pacing in CRT: QS in V1, R in lead I; always compare with the reference ECG.

prog-dai-058.question: In a CRT "non-responder" at 6 months, what is the first step?
options: Explant the LV lead and revert to RV-only pacing
Check % BiV pacing, LV capture, arrhythmias and medical therapy
Upgrade straight away to CRT-D to improve response
Program the maximum AV delay to respect native conduction
commentaires: Incorrect: CRT is not abandoned before looking for correctable causes of non-response.
Correct: correctable causes are sought first, before any echocardiographic optimisation of delays.
Incorrect: the defibrillator does not treat non-response to resynchronisation.
Incorrect: a long AV delay promotes intrinsic conduction and loss of biventricular pacing.
prog-dai-058.explication: About one third of patients do not respond to CRT. Before concluding that it has failed, correctable causes are sought: incomplete biventricular pacing (AF, PVCs, inappropriate AV delay), loss of LV capture or phrenic nerve stimulation that led to the output being reduced, an unfavourable LV lead position (apical or anterior), insufficient medical therapy or volume overload. Multidisciplinary care improves these outcomes. Echocardiographic optimisation of AV/VV delays comes later, on a case-by-case basis. Upgrading to CRT-D does not treat non-response.
prog-dai-058.aRetenir: CRT non-responder: first check % BiV pacing, LV capture, arrhythmias and medical therapy, then the delays.

prog-dai-059.question: True or false: routine echocardiographic optimisation of AV and VV delays is recommended in all patients after CRT implantation.
options: True
False
