commentaires: Incorrect: randomised trials have not shown any benefit from routine echocardiographic optimisation.
Correct: programming is empirical, and guided optimisation is reserved for non-responders.
prog-dai-059.explication: False: randomised trials have not shown any benefit from routine echocardiographic optimisation of AV/VV delays compared with empirical programming. In practice, an AV delay short enough to ensure biventricular capture without truncating atrial filling is programmed, and guided optimisation (echocardiography, ECG, automatic algorithms) is reserved for non-responders. The pitfall is to invest considerable resources for an unproven benefit, instead of first checking the pacing percentage and LV capture.
prog-dai-059.aRetenir: AV/VV optimisation: not routine, reserved for non-responders.

prog-dai-060.question: A patient with an LVEF of 35% and high-grade AV block requires ventricular pacing. What do the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend?
options: CRT rather than RV pacing, regardless of NYHA class
Dual-chamber pacemaker with conventional apical RV pacing
Single-chamber VVI pacemaker programmed at 40 bpm
No pacemaker as long as the patient remains asymptomatic
commentaires: Correct: LVEF < 40% and a need for ventricular pacing = CRT rather than RV pacing (class I in 2021, IIa in the 2026 ESC HF guidelines), even in AF.
Incorrect: in a patient with LVEF < 40%, frequent RV pacing worsens LV dysfunction.
Incorrect: VVI at 40 bpm is inappropriate for high-grade AV block and does not correct dyssynchrony.
Incorrect: high-grade AV block is an indication for pacing, even in a patient with few symptoms.
prog-dai-060.explication: In a patient with reduced LVEF who needs ventricular pacing for high-grade AV block, the 2021 ESC guidelines (cardiac pacing and CRT) recommend CRT rather than RV pacing (class I, level A, for LVEF < 40%), including in AF and regardless of NYHA class. Isolated RV pacing, even with a dual-chamber device, creates LBBB-type dyssynchrony that worsens LV dysfunction, especially if it is near-continuous. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines keep the same message, regardless of NYHA class and QRS width, but as class IIa (level B1), and for all HFrEF, now defined as LVEF < 50%. VVI at 40 bpm or no pacing would be inappropriate for high-grade AV block, even with few symptoms. Conduction system pacing is an evolving alternative; the 2026 ESC HF guidelines make no recommendation on it in the absence of a randomised trial with clinical endpoints.
prog-dai-060.aRetenir: Reduced LVEF + high-grade AV block = CRT rather than RV pacing (ESC 2021: class I; ESC 2026 HF: class IIa).

prog-dai-061.question: True or false: in a patient with a conventional pacemaker and a high burden of RV pacing who develops symptomatic heart failure with LVEF ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy, an upgrade to CRT should be considered.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: upgrade to CRT should be considered (class IIa) in RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.
Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines do recommend considering upgrade (IIa), confirmed by the 2026 ESC HF guidelines, weighing up the procedural risk.
prog-dai-061.explication: True: the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering upgrade to CRT (class IIa) in this setting of RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines confirm class IIa (level B1) in patients with LVEF ≤ 35% and a significant proportion of RV pacing whose HF worsens despite optimal therapy. They are based on BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade, the first randomised trial on this subject: with ≥ 20% RV pacing and a paced QRS ≥ 150 ms, upgrade to CRT-D reduced the primary composite endpoint of death, HF hospitalisation and absence of reverse remodelling (HR 0.27). The 2026 ESC guidelines also recommend checking the proportion of RV pacing in any device recipient with new-onset or worsening HFrEF (class IIa). Upgrade (or conduction system pacing) restores more physiological ventricular activation. The procedural risk, which is higher than at de novo implantation, must be weighed up.
prog-dai-061.aRetenir: RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy with LVEF ≤ 35%: CRT upgrade (IIa, BUDAPEST-CRT Upgrade); always check the % RV pacing.

prog-dai-062.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, how should one choose between CRT-P and CRT-D in a patient with an indication for CRT?
options: CRT-D routinely in all patients eligible for resynchronisation
CRT-D reserved for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy
CRT-P routinely over the age of 75, whatever the context
CRT-D if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, shared decision
commentaires: Incorrect: in the absence of an ICD indication, the choice is individualised (class IIa).
Incorrect: the opposite is true; the benefit of the defibrillator tends to be smaller in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy (DANISH).
Incorrect: no strict age cut-off is set; age is only one element of the decision.
Correct: CRT-D is recommended (class I) if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, the decision is made case by case.
prog-dai-062.explication: If the patient has an ICD indication (secondary prevention, ischaemic heart disease with LVEF ≤ 35%), a CRT-D is recommended (class I). Otherwise, the choice is made on a case-by-case basis (class IIa): age, comorbidities, aetiology (smaller benefit of the defibrillator in non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy, especially in older patients, as suggested by DANISH), fibrosis on MRI and patient preference. CRT-P is simpler, less costly and carries no risk of inappropriate shocks. No strict age cut-off is set.
prog-dai-062.aRetenir: CRT-D if there is an ICD indication; otherwise, an individualised, shared decision.

prog-dai-063.question: Which trial showed, in NYHA III–IV patients, a reduction in all-cause mortality with CRT-D compared with medical therapy, whereas the mortality reduction with CRT-P did not reach statistical significance?
options: CARE-HF
COMPANION
EchoCRT
MADIT-CRT
commentaires: Incorrect: CARE-HF showed that CRT-P alone reduces mortality; it had no CRT-D arm.
Correct: significant mortality reduction with CRT-D, borderline significance with CRT-P.
Incorrect: EchoCRT involved patients with a narrow QRS and was stopped for futility.
Incorrect: MADIT-CRT involved mildly symptomatic patients (NYHA I–II), CRT-D versus ICD alone.
prog-dai-063.explication: COMPANION compared medical therapy, CRT-P and CRT-D in NYHA III–IV patients with QRS ≥ 120 ms. Both forms of CRT reduced the endpoint of death or hospitalisation. For all-cause mortality, the reduction was significant with CRT-D and of borderline significance with CRT-P. CARE-HF, published later, demonstrated that CRT-P alone reduces mortality. MADIT-CRT involved mildly symptomatic patients (NYHA I–II), and EchoCRT patients with a narrow QRS.
prog-dai-063.aRetenir: COMPANION: CRT-D reduces mortality; CARE-HF: so does CRT-P.

prog-dai-064.question: Which patients were enrolled in MADIT-CRT, and which subgroup benefited most?
options: NYHA III–IV, LVEF ≤ 35%, QRS ≥ 120 ms; benefit mainly with RBBB
NYHA I–II, LVEF ≤ 30%, QRS ≥ 130 ms; benefit mainly with LBBB
NYHA II–III, LVEF ≤ 40%, QRS ≥ 150 ms; benefit mainly in AF
NYHA I–II, LVEF ≤ 35%, QRS < 130 ms; benefit in women
commentaires: Incorrect: MADIT-CRT specifically enrolled mildly symptomatic patients, and the benefit concerned LBBB.
Correct: mildly symptomatic patients, CRT-D versus ICD alone, with the benefit concentrated in LBBB.
Incorrect: LVEF ≤ 30%, not 40%, and patients in permanent AF were not the target of the trial.
Incorrect: MADIT-CRT enrolled only patients with QRS ≥ 130 ms; a narrow QRS does not warrant CRT.
prog-dai-064.explication: MADIT-CRT compared CRT-D with ICD alone in mildly symptomatic patients (ischaemic NYHA I or NYHA II), with LVEF ≤ 30% and QRS ≥ 130 ms. CRT-D reduced heart failure events by about one third, and this benefit was concentrated in patients with LBBB. This trial extended CRT to mildly symptomatic patients. It reinforced the idea that LBBB morphology is the best predictor of response.
prog-dai-064.aRetenir: MADIT-CRT: CRT is beneficial from NYHA I–II, especially with LBBB.

prog-dai-065.question: Which ECG criteria are classically sought to confirm left bundle branch capture during left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP)?
options: LBBB pattern in V1, long LV activation time in V6
Paced QRS > 200 ms, with a left-sided delay pattern
qR in V1, short and stable LV activation time in V6
No visible spike and a QRS identical to the intrinsic one
commentaires: Incorrect: this pattern reflects deep septal pacing without left bundle branch capture.
Incorrect: such a broad QRS suggests slow myocardial pacing, far from conduction system capture.
Correct: right-sided delay in V1 (qR, rSR') and a short stimulus to R-wave peak time in V6 that remains constant as output is varied.
Incorrect: a QRS identical to the intrinsic one with no spike reflects absence of pacing.
prog-dai-065.explication: By directly capturing the left bundle branch, pacing rapidly activates the LV, while the RV is activated later: this produces a right-sided delay pattern in V1 (qR, rSR'). The time from stimulus to R-wave peak in V6 (LV activation time) is short and remains stable as output is varied. Commonly proposed thresholds are around 75 to 80 ms depending on the baseline QRS. An LBBB pattern with slow LV activation, on the contrary, reflects deep septal pacing without bundle branch capture. The transition between non-selective and selective capture is also a strong criterion.
prog-dai-065.aRetenir: LBBAP: right-sided delay in V1 and a short, stable LV activation time in V6.

prog-dai-066.question: According to the 2023 HRS/APHRS/LAHRS guideline, in a patient with LVEF between 36 and 50% who needs ventricular pacing and is expected to have more than 40% pacing, which strategy is preferable?
options: Conventional apical or septal RV pacing
Conduction system or biventricular pacing
No ventricular pacing, to preserve the LVEF
Single-chamber ICD with backup RV pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: in these patients, frequent RV pacing carries a risk of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy.
Correct: class 2a (HRS 2023) for preferring physiological pacing (His bundle, LBBAP or biventricular).
Incorrect: the patient needs ventricular pacing; forgoing it is not an option.
Incorrect: the question concerns the pacing mode, not an indication for a defibrillator.
prog-dai-066.explication: The 2023 HRS guideline on physiological pacing considers it reasonable (class 2a) to prefer more physiological pacing (His bundle, LBBAP or biventricular) over apical or septal RV pacing in patients with LVEF of 36 to 50% who need frequent ventricular pacing (> 40%). These patients are at risk of RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy; forgoing pacing is not an option since it is indicated. In Europe, the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines now include these LVEF values within HFrEF (< 50%) and recommend CRT rather than RV pacing in high-grade AV block (class IIa), without making any recommendation on conduction system pacing in the absence of a randomised trial. The 2025 ESC consensus considers it a reasonable option in AV block regardless of LVEF. The ICD is not at issue here, only pacing.
prog-dai-066.aRetenir: LVEF 36–50% and ventricular pacing > 40%: prefer physiological pacing to RV pacing.

prog-dai-067.question: What is the classic drawback of His bundle pacing compared with left bundle branch area pacing?
options: A paced QRS broader than with apical RV pacing
A higher risk of septal perforation
Inability to correct left bundle branch block
Higher, sometimes rising, capture thresholds
commentaires: Incorrect: His bundle pacing, on the contrary, gives the narrowest QRS and the most physiological activation.
Incorrect: septal perforation is rather a concern with LBBAP, whose lead is screwed deep into the septum.
Incorrect: it can correct some proximal LBBBs.
Correct: small, fibrous target area, higher and unstable thresholds, hence faster battery depletion.
prog-dai-067.explication: His bundle pacing gives the most physiological activation, but the lead is placed on a small, fibrous area. Thresholds are often higher, sometimes rising over time, and sensed R waves may be small (with a risk of atrial oversensing). This results in faster battery depletion and more frequent reinterventions. LBBAP, with a lead screwed deep into the septum, offers lower, stable thresholds. The risk of septal perforation, in fact, concerns LBBAP rather than His bundle pacing. His bundle pacing can correct some proximal LBBBs.
prog-dai-067.aRetenir: His bundle pacing: ideal activation, but higher and unstable thresholds.

prog-dai-068.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, what is the role of His bundle pacing in a CRT candidate in whom the LV lead could not be placed in the coronary sinus?
options: Contraindicated (class III) owing to a lack of randomised data
A bailout option to be considered (class IIa)
Recommended first-line instead of CRT (class I)
Not addressed by the 2021 ESC guidelines
commentaires: Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines include it as an option when LV lead placement fails.
Correct: class IIa when LV lead placement fails, alongside other options such as a surgical epicardial lead.
Incorrect: this document does not recommend it first-line instead of biventricular CRT.
Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines explicitly address His bundle pacing.
prog-dai-068.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines give His bundle pacing a class IIa recommendation as a bailout option in a CRT candidate when LV lead placement in the coronary sinus fails, alongside other options such as a surgical epicardial lead. In this document, it is not recommended first-line instead of biventricular CRT, given the lack of sufficient randomised trials at the time. The 2023 HRS guideline takes the same line for conduction system pacing (His bundle or LBBAP) when biventricular CRT fails or is ineffective. The 2025 ESC consensus on indications for conduction system pacing also advises it as a bailout after LV lead failure, with LBBAP now the most widely used. The 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines, for their part, make no recommendation on conduction system pacing, in the absence of a randomised trial with clinical endpoints.
prog-dai-068.aRetenir: Failed LV lead placement: conduction system pacing as a bailout (His IIa in ESC 2021; 2025 ESC consensus).

prog-dai-069.question: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, in which situations should adding a backup RV lead be considered in a patient with His bundle pacing?
prog-dai-069.reponseAttendue: Pacing-dependent patient; high-grade AV block or infranodal (infra-Hisian) block; high or unstable His capture threshold; planned AV junction ablation ("pace and ablate" strategy).
prog-dai-069.explication: The His bundle lead may lose capture (high or rising threshold) or become ineffective if the conduction disorder progresses distal to the pacing site, in the case of infranodal block. In a dependent patient, this can be serious. The 2021 ESC guidelines therefore propose considering a backup RV lead (class IIa) in dependent patients, in high-grade or infranodal AV block, with a high capture threshold, or when AV junction ablation is planned. This lead is also used for sensing, which is often better than with the His bundle lead. Programming must then be adapted to this configuration (class I recommendation).
prog-dai-069.aRetenir: His bundle pacing in a dependent patient or with distal block: plan a backup RV lead.

prog-dai-070.question: What is the main aim of conduction system pacing (His bundle or left bundle branch) compared with conventional RV pacing?
options: To reduce device cost and procedure time
To allow more effective defibrillation shocks
To remove the need for an atrial lead in a patient in sinus rhythm
To activate the ventricles via the native His–Purkinje system
commentaires: Incorrect: hardware cost is similar to conventional pacing, and the procedure involves a learning curve.
Incorrect: conduction system pacing is not designed for defibrillation.
Incorrect: an atrial lead is still needed if AV synchrony is desired.
Correct: rapid, synchronous activation, without the LBBB-type dyssynchrony of RV pacing.
prog-dai-070.explication: Apical or septal RV pacing activates the ventricles slowly, from cell to cell, with an LBBB pattern and dyssynchrony that can impair LVEF in the long term. Conduction system pacing uses the native His–Purkinje system, for rapid, synchronous activation with a narrow or only slightly widened QRS. It does not remove the need for an atrial lead if AV synchrony is desired, and it is not designed for defibrillation. Its hardware cost is similar to that of conventional pacing, but it involves a learning curve.
prog-dai-070.aRetenir: Conduction system pacing = physiological ventricular activation, without the dyssynchrony of RV pacing.

prog-dai-071.question: Which complication is more specific to left bundle branch area pacing (LBBAP) than to conventional RV pacing?
options: Phrenic nerve stimulation
Pacemaker syndrome
Septal perforation into the LV
Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia
commentaires: Incorrect: phrenic nerve stimulation mainly concerns the LV lead in the coronary sinus.
Incorrect: it is related to loss of AV synchrony, not to the ventricular pacing site.
Correct: the lead, screwed deep into the septum, can break through into the LV cavity.
Incorrect: it depends on retrograde conduction and the PVARP, not on the pacing site.
prog-dai-071.explication: In LBBAP, the lead is screwed deep into the interventricular septum, from the right side towards the left. Excessive penetration can result in septal perforation, with the lead emerging into the LV cavity: loss of capture, a pure LV pacing pattern, a theoretical embolic risk. During the procedure, impedance and the current of injury are monitored to avoid this complication. Phrenic nerve stimulation mainly concerns the LV lead in the coronary sinus. Pacemaker syndrome and pacemaker-mediated tachycardia are not related to the ventricular pacing site.
prog-dai-071.aRetenir: LBBAP: beware of septal perforation while screwing in the lead.

prog-dai-072.question: Why is ATP programmed before shocks in the VT zone of an ICD?
options: Because ATP is more effective than shocks for VF
Because ATP is painless and terminates many VTs

commentaires: Incorrect: ATP is ineffective for VF, which has no organised circuit; the VF zone relies on shocks.
Correct: it terminates a large proportion of monomorphic VTs and avoids a painful shock.

prog-dai-072.explication: ATP consists of a short burst of pacing faster than the VT, which the patient generally does not feel, or feels very little. It terminates a large proportion of monomorphic VTs, including fast VTs, and thus avoids a painful, distressing and energy-consuming shock. If it fails, the ICD moves on to the next therapy (another ATP, then a shock). ATP is not effective for VF, which has no organised circuit: this is why the VF zone relies on shocks.
prog-dai-072.aRetenir: ATP first: painless and effective for most monomorphic VTs.

prog-dai-073.question: What is meant by a "monitor zone" in an ICD?
prog-dai-073.reponseAttendue: A rate range in which episodes are detected and stored, without any therapy (ATP or shock) being delivered.
prog-dai-073.explication: A monitor zone detects and stores episodes within a given rate range, without delivering therapy. It can, for example, reveal slow VTs or SVTs, which can then be reviewed in clinic or via remote monitoring. It is useful in primary prevention, where therapy zones are set high. Confusing it with a therapy zone is a pitfall: an episode in the monitor zone will never be treated by the device.
prog-dai-073.aRetenir: Monitor zone = record, do not treat.

prog-dai-074.question: True or false: in PainFree SST, despite modern discrimination algorithms and appropriate programming, the one-year inappropriate shock rate remained above 5%, in single-chamber as well as dual- or triple-chamber devices.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the observed rates were much lower, around 1.5% in dual- or triple-chamber devices and 2.5% in single-chamber devices.
Correct: with modern programming and discriminators, one-year inappropriate shocks remained below 3%.
prog-dai-074.explication: False: PainFree SST evaluated a suite of discrimination and noise rejection algorithms combined with "smart" programming. One-year inappropriate shock rates were around 1.5% with dual- or triple-chamber ICDs and 2.5% with single-chamber ICDs, i.e. below 3% in all cases. These figures are much lower than those of the early ICD trials. They show that modern programming and discriminators greatly reduce the problem, without eliminating it.
prog-dai-074.aRetenir: With modern programming, inappropriate shocks become rare (≈ 1.5–2.5% per year).
